title: The Voynich Manuscript (Beinecke MS 408) and its script
otherNames: Beinecke MS 408 (Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University)
Voynichese (the informal name for the script and its 'language')
EVA, the European (later 'Extensible') Voynich Alphabet: the Latin-letter transcription alphabet of Gabriel Landini and René Zandbergen (1998)
The 'Roger Bacon cipher manuscript' (how Voynich and W. R. Newbold presented it; the Bacon attribution is legend, see claims)
family: Not a magical alphabet with a known key. It is an unread script known from one manuscript, with no Unicode encoding and no accepted sound values. It stands in the Magical Scriptorium beside the secret and cipher alphabets of the 15th–17th centuries because it is the most famous unread script in the European tradition. The manuscript itself has astrological and herbal pictures. No link to Trithemius, Agrippa or the angelic alphabets is documented.
summary: Beinecke MS 408 at Yale is a small illustrated codex on vellum, about 240 pages, written throughout in a script found nowhere else. In 2009 the University of Arizona radiocarbon-dated its vellum to 1404–1438. It is documented in Prague from 1639 (Georg Baresch). Johannes Marcus Marci sent it to Athanasius Kircher in Rome with a letter dated 19 August 1665 or 1666, and the bookseller Wilfrid Voynich bought it from the Jesuits in 1912. Readers have proposed a cipher, a natural language in an invented script, a constructed language and a meaningless hoax. None of these readings is accepted.

firstAttestation.work: The manuscript itself, the only known witness of the script. The earliest document that mentions it is a letter from Georg Baresch to Athanasius Kircher, 1639.
firstAttestation.author: Unknown. The authors suggested in the 17th century (Roger Bacon) and the 20th (Dee, Kelley and others) are legend or hypothesis; see claims.
firstAttestation.date: Vellum: 1404–1438, by radiocarbon dating of four samples (University of Arizona, Greg Hodgins; samples taken in 2009, result announced by the university in February 2011). The writing is not dated directly. The ink analysis made at the same time (McCrone Associates) found nothing inconsistent with that period. First documentary mention: Baresch's letter to Kircher, dated, as I recall, 27 April 1639.
firstAttestation.place: Unknown. Central Europe and northern Italy have been proposed, from the costumes, the castle with swallow-tail battlements on the 'rosettes' foldout, and the Romance month names on the zodiac pages. None of these settles it. Documented in Prague by 1639.
firstAttestation.locator: Beinecke Rare Book and Manuscript Library, Yale University, MS 408. A later hand numbered the leaves up to f. 116. About 14 numbered leaves are missing (as I recall, ff. 12, 59–64, 74, 91–92, 97–98 and 109–110), which leaves about 102. There are several foldouts. The Marci letter is kept with the manuscript.
firstAttestation.notes: Radiocarbon dates the death of the animals whose skins became the vellum, not the writing. Most scholars take the writing to be close to that date, because vellum was rarely stored for decades, but this is an inference. Before 2009, dates from the 13th century (Bacon) to the 16th (Panofsky, as reported in D'Imperio 1978) had been proposed. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.author: Unknown scribes. Prescott Currier (1976) saw at least two hands; Lisa Fagin Davis (2020) argued for five.
transmission.what: Radiocarbon date of the vellum. The script, the illustrations and the text were made on it at an unknown date, presumably soon after. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.work: Beinecke MS 408, f. 1r, inscription at the foot of the page
transmission.author: Jacobus Horcicky de Tepenec (Jakub Hořčický z Tepence, also called Sinapius), chemist and pharmacist at Rudolf II's court
transmission.what: A faint inscription reading 'Jacobj à Tepenece', now legible only under ultraviolet light. Horcicky took the predicate 'de Tepenec' when he was ennobled in 1608, so the inscription cannot be earlier. He died in 1622. Whether it is his signature, or an owner's note added by someone else, is debated (Zandbergen, in Clemens 2016). Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.author: reported by Raphael Mnishovsky (Rafael Soběhrd Mišovský, d. 1644) to Marci
transmission.what: Says that Emperor Rudolf II (reigned 1576–1612) owned the book and paid 600 ducats for it. No other document confirms this; no record of the purchase in Rudolf's papers was found. Report it as Marci's hearsay. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.work: Letter of Georg Baresch to Athanasius Kircher, among Kircher's correspondence in the archive of the Pontifical Gregorian University, Rome
transmission.author: Georg Baresch (Baresius), Prague
transmission.what: The earliest document that mentions the manuscript. Baresch, who owned it, asks Kircher for help in reading it. Kircher's Coptic book (Prodromus coptus, 1636) had made him the obvious person to ask. As I recall, Baresch had already sent Kircher a sample copied from it. The letter was found in the 2000s; I could not check by whom. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.author: Georg Baresch → Johannes Marcus Marci
transmission.what: Marci's 1665/6 letter says the book was left to him in the will of 'a very close friend'. This is generally identified as Baresch, who died about 1662 (date from memory). Some accounts put a stage between Baresch and Marci; this is not settled. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.date: 19 August 1665 or 1666 (the last digit of the year is unclear)
transmission.work: Letter of Johannes Marcus Marci (Jan Marek Marci, 1595–1667) to Athanasius Kircher, Prague; it travelled with the book and is kept with it at the Beinecke
transmission.author: Johannes Marcus Marci, physician and rector of the University of Prague
transmission.what: Sends the book to Kircher in Rome. Repeats Mnishovsky's story of Rudolf II, the 600 ducats and Roger Bacon as author, and, as I recall, says that Marci himself suspends judgement. Voynich reported finding the letter with the manuscript after 1912. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.work: Library of the Collegio Romano, Rome
transmission.author: Athanasius Kircher (d. 1680) and the Jesuits
transmission.what: Kircher never published anything on the manuscript, and no answer from him to Marci about it is known to me. It stayed in Jesuit hands. After the Italian state took over Rome (1870) and seized Jesuit property, part of the library, this book included, was reportedly kept as the private property of the Jesuit General Petrus Beckx and later moved to the Villa Mondragone at Frascati. This stage is from memory, at medium-low confidence. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.work: Purchase at the Villa Mondragone, Frascati
transmission.author: Wilfrid M. Voynich (Michał Habdank-Wojnicz, 1865–1930), antiquarian bookseller in London and later New York
transmission.what: Voynich bought the manuscript from the Jesuits, with other manuscripts. For years he kept the source secret. He promoted it as a work of Roger Bacon, and the manuscript has carried his name ever since. The Voynich 100 conference was held at Villa Mondragone in 2012 for the centenary (medium confidence). Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.work: Lecture in Philadelphia (April 1921; the month is from memory); The Cipher of Roger Bacon, ed. Roland Grubb Kent (Philadelphia: University of Pennsylvania Press, 1928)
transmission.author: William Romaine Newbold (1865–1926)
transmission.what: The first well-known claim to have deciphered it. Newbold read microscopic 'shorthand' strokes as a Latin text by Bacon. John Matthews Manly showed in 1931 (Speculum 6) that the strokes are cracking of the ink, and that the method could produce whatever text one wanted. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.author: Ethel Lilian Voynich (d. 1960) and Anne Nill; H. P. Kraus
transmission.what: After Voynich died in 1930, the manuscript passed to his widow Ethel and to his secretary Anne Nill. Kraus, the New York dealer, bought it in 1961 (for $24,500, a figure from memory). He could not sell it, and in 1969 he gave it to Yale's Beinecke Library, where it is MS 408. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.work: Friedman's first and second Voynich study groups
transmission.author: William F. Friedman (with Elizebeth Friedman and wartime colleagues)
transmission.what: Professional cryptanalysts made a full transcription (the 'FSG' alphabet) and analysed it statistically, without finding a solution. Friedman came to think it an early a priori constructed language; see quotations. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.work: J. H. Tiltman, NSA Technical Journal (1967); P. H. Currier, papers at the 1976 seminar; M. E. D'Imperio, The Voynich Manuscript: An Elegant Enigma (NSA, 1978)
transmission.author: John Tiltman; Prescott Currier; Mary D'Imperio
transmission.what: Tiltman described the regular structure of the words. Currier found that the herbal pages fall into two statistically distinct 'languages', Currier A and B, which go with different hands. D'Imperio's monograph is still the standard survey of research up to 1978. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.work: EVA; the interlinear transcription file; the Takahashi transcription
transmission.author: Gabriel Landini and René Zandbergen (EVA); Jorge Stolfi (interlinear file); Takeshi Takahashi (complete transcription)
transmission.what: EVA gave the script a stroke-based Latin-letter transcription that could be pronounced. It was designed to record what is on the page without deciding which strokes form one glyph. The machine-readable transcriptions that followed are the basis of most later statistics. Zandbergen later maintained a revised transcription and file format (the ZL transcription, IVTFF). Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.work: 'An Elegant Hoax? A Possible Solution to the Voynich Manuscript', Cryptologia 28; Scientific American, July 2004
transmission.author: Gordon Rugg
transmission.what: Showed that a table of word parts and a grille (a card with holes, of the kind Cardano published in 1550) can produce text with many Voynich-like features. He offered this as a possible hoax method, not as proof. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.work: Radiocarbon dating and ink analysis, made for an Austrian television documentary
transmission.author: Greg Hodgins and team, University of Arizona AMS Laboratory; McCrone Associates (inks)
transmission.what: Dated the vellum to 1404–1438. This rules out authorship by Roger Bacon (d. c. 1292). It also means that a forgery by Dee, Kelley or Voynich would have needed a stock of century-old blank vellum. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.author: M. A. Montemurro and D. H. Zanette (PLoS ONE, 2013); T. Timm and A. Schinner (Cryptologia, 2020); L. Fagin Davis (Manuscript Studies, 2020)
transmission.what: Montemurro and Zanette found words clustering by section, as keywords do in real texts. Timm and Schinner proposed that the text was generated by copying and altering earlier words ('self-citation'). Fagin Davis identified five scribal hands. These are the main recent lines of scholarship; none reads the text. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

transmission.work: The Voynich Manuscript, ed. Raymond Clemens (New Haven: Yale University Press with the Beinecke Library)
transmission.author: Raymond Clemens (ed.); introduction by Deborah E. Harkness; essays including René Zandbergen on the earliest owners
transmission.what: The authorised full-colour facsimile, with essays on provenance, the physical book and the history of attempts to read it. The best single printed source for the page. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: The vellum of MS 408 dates from 1404–1438.
claims.evidence: Radiocarbon dating of four samples by the University of Arizona (Hodgins), 2009; announced in February 2011. It dates the skin, not the writing. Details of the individual samples and confidence intervals were not checked in this run. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).
sources: University of Arizona press release, February 2011
Hodgins, paper at the Voynich 100 conference, Frascati, 2012 (medium confidence)

claims.claim: The ink and paint show nothing inconsistent with a 15th-century date.
claims.evidence: Analysis by McCrone Associates, 2009, made in the same project as the radiocarbon tests. I did not check whether a full report was published. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: Georg Baresch of Prague owned the manuscript by 1639 and asked Kircher to help read it.
claims.evidence: Baresch's letter to Kircher (1639), in Kircher's correspondence, Pontifical Gregorian University. Marci's letters to Kircher are also relevant. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: Marci sent the manuscript to Kircher with a letter dated 19 August 1665 or 1666.
claims.evidence: The letter itself, kept with MS 408. The year is ambiguous in the letter, so both dates are given. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).
sources: Beinecke MS 408 and the Marci letter

claims.claim: Emperor Rudolf II owned the manuscript and paid 600 ducats for it.
claims.evidence: Only Marci's letter says so, and Marci gives it as what Raphael Mnishovsky told him. It is hearsay, at least a generation after Rudolf's death (1612). No independent record is known to me. The Horcicky inscription (if genuine) puts the book among Rudolf's courtiers, but does not prove that Rudolf owned it. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

Mnishovsky's opinion as reported by Marci; taken up by Voynich and by Newbold (1921, 1928). Bacon died about 1292, so the radiocarbon date of the vellum (1404–1438) rules him out, unless the text is a later copy of a work of his, which no evidence supports. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: John Dee brought the manuscript to Prague and sold it to Rudolf II.
claims.evidence: A conjecture of Voynich's, repeated by many since. It is often connected with an entry in Dee's diary recording that he received 630 ducats in October 1586; that entry does not name any book (from memory, low confidence). No document puts the manuscript in Dee's hands. Present it as a hypothesis, with this weakness. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: Edward Kelley (or Dee, or Voynich) forged the manuscript.
claims.evidence: Proposed at various times as a hoax hypothesis. It is not refuted outright, but since 2009 any such forger would have needed blank vellum a century or more old, and the inks match the period. The Baresch letter of 1639 rules out Voynich. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: The f1r inscription is Jacobus Horcicky de Tepenec's signature.
claims.evidence: The inscription 'Jacobj à Tepenece' is real and visible under UV light. Whether it is in Horcicky's own hand, or is an owner's note written by another person (perhaps a later owner or librarian), has been debated. Compare it with his known signatures before calling it a signature. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: Newbold deciphered the manuscript as a work of Roger Bacon (1921).
claims.evidence: Refuted by John Matthews Manly in Speculum 6 (1931). The microscopic 'shorthand' was cracking of the ink, and the anagramming method had no fixed rules. No one has defended Newbold since. Standing 'disputed' is used for a claim that was made and has been rejected. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: The text falls into two statistically distinct varieties ('Currier A' and 'Currier B').
claims.evidence: Currier's 1976 analysis. Different word and glyph frequencies mark sections in different hands. Later statistics confirm it, and the finding is widely accepted. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).
sources: Currier 1976, in D'Imperio (ed.), New Research on the Voynich Manuscript (1976)

claims.evidence: Lisa Fagin Davis's palaeographical study (Manuscript Studies, 2020), building on Currier's two hands. It is a scholarly finding that others are still testing, not a consensus. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: The text has some statistical features of natural language.
claims.evidence: Word frequencies roughly follow Zipf's law, and some words cluster in particular sections as topic words do (Montemurro and Zanette 2013). These are measurements. Whether they show that the text has meaning is disputed: a careful generating method could produce some of them. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: The text also has features that are unusual for European languages.
claims.evidence: Glyph-pair entropy is low (Bennett 1976). Words are built from rigid slots, and Stolfi described their structure as a paradigm. One- and two-glyph words are scarce, and long words are absent. The same or nearly the same word often repeats two or three times in a row. These measurements are the main obstacle to every proposed reading. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: Hypothesis: a cipher (a known language, encrypted).
claims.evidence: Held by Newbold, by Leonell Strong (1945), by Robert Brumbaugh (1970s) and by others, each with a different system. Simple substitution is unlikely, because it would keep the letter statistics of the plaintext language, and the Voynich statistics match no known language. The ciphers attested before about 1440 that could give the observed word structure are few. No proposed cipher has produced connected text that someone else could reproduce. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: Hypothesis: a natural language written in an invented script.
claims.evidence: Many languages have been proposed. Among them: an East Asian or tonal language (suggested on statistical grounds, among others by Stolfi); Nahuatl, from the plants (Tucker and Talbert, HerbalGram, 2013), though the vellum date is pre-Columbian; Hebrew (Hauer and Kondrak, computational, 2016–2018); a proto-Romance language (Cheshire, Romance Studies, 2019, rejected by medievalists, and the press release of his university was withdrawn); abbreviated Latin (Gibbs, TLS, 2017, rejected by specialists); and Stephen Bax's partial reading of a few names (2014). None has given verifiable connected text. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

Held by William Friedman and John Tiltman: an a priori 'philosophical' language whose words are built by classification, which would explain the rigid word structure. The objection is that the known a priori language schemes are 17th-century (e.g. Wilkins, 1668), and nothing like them is known from the early 15th. The hypothesis cannot be tested without a key. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: Hypothesis: meaningless text (a hoax, or glossolalia).
claims.evidence: Rugg (2004) showed that a table-and-grille method could make text like this. Schinner (2007) argued that the statistics point to a stochastic process, and Timm and Schinner (2020) proposed a self-citation method. Kennedy and Churchill (2004) suggested glossolalia. The objections: the 15th-century date, the great labour involved, the clustering of words by section, and the Currier A/B distinction. Rugg's grille is a format Cardano published in 1550, though Rugg argues simpler tools would do. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

claims.claim: The zodiac pages have month names in a Romance language, written in Latin script.
claims.evidence: The month names are there, in a hand different from the main script, and possibly later. Their language (Occitan, Catalan and French have each been proposed) is disputed, and so is whether the person who added them knew the original text. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: EVA o
letters.value: No accepted value. EVA letters are labels chosen because the glyph looks like them, not sound values.
letters.form: A small closed loop at x-height, round or slightly oval, the same size as the bowl of EVA a. It looks like a Latin minuscule o. Pen direction was not checked; draw it as a single closed curve with an even stroke.
letters.note: Among the commonest glyphs. Very frequent at the start of words (ol, or, ok-, ot-) and after q (qo-). Find it in 'ol' and 'qokeedy'. The ranking by frequency is approximate and from memory; recount it from a transcription file (Takahashi, or Zandbergen's ZL/IVTFF) before printing any numbers. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: EVA e
letters.value: No accepted value. EVA letters are labels chosen because the glyph looks like them, not sound values.
letters.form: A small c: one open curve at x-height, open to the right, like a Latin c. It may have a very small upward tick at its top end. It is narrower than the ch 'bench' (unit 3) and is not joined to its neighbour at the top. It is often doubled (ee) and sometimes tripled.
letters.note: Find it in 'chedy', 'shedy', 'qokeedy'. Whether the top tick is always there was not checked; leave it off unless the traced folio shows it. EVA uses the letter e for this glyph; it does not mean the sound e. The ranking by frequency is approximate and from memory; recount it from a transcription file (Takahashi, or Zandbergen's ZL/IVTFF) before printing any numbers. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: EVA ch (the 'bench')
letters.value: No accepted value. EVA letters are labels chosen because the glyph looks like them, not sound values.
letters.form: Two c-shaped curves side by side, both open to the right, at x-height. Their tops are joined by one short horizontal or slightly arched stroke running from the top of the left c to the top of the right c. The whole is about twice the width of EVA e. EVA writes it as two letters (c + h) because it splits glyphs into strokes, but in the manuscript it behaves as one unit.
letters.note: Very common, at the start and inside words: 'chedy', 'chol', 'chor', 'chey'. EVA c and h almost never occur except in ch, sh and the benched gallows (unit 19). The name 'bench' is the usual name among Voynich researchers; I could not check who coined it. The ranking by frequency is approximate and from memory; recount it from a transcription file (Takahashi, or Zandbergen's ZL/IVTFF) before printing any numbers. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: EVA y
letters.value: No accepted value. EVA letters are labels chosen because the glyph looks like them, not sound values.
letters.form: Like EVA a (unit 5), but the stroke on the right of the bowl runs well below the baseline and curves back to the left at its foot, so the glyph looks like a numeral 9. The bowl sits at x-height; the tail is about as long as the bowl is tall.
letters.note: Very common at the end of words ('-dy', '-ey', 'chedy', 'qokeedy'), and also found at the start of words. The older First Study Group and Currier transcriptions wrote this glyph as '9' (medium confidence, from memory). The ranking by frequency is approximate and from memory; recount it from a transcription file (Takahashi, or Zandbergen's ZL/IVTFF) before printing any numbers. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: EVA a
letters.value: No accepted value. EVA letters are labels chosen because the glyph looks like them, not sound values.
letters.form: A small round bowl like EVA o, with a short straight down-stroke against its right side that reaches the baseline and may end in a slight flick to the right. It looks like a one-storey Latin minuscule a. No stroke rises above x-height.
letters.note: Usually followed by i, l, r or n: 'aiin', 'daiin', 'al', 'ar', 'dar'. The ranking by frequency is approximate and from memory; recount it from a transcription file (Takahashi, or Zandbergen's ZL/IVTFF) before printing any numbers. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: EVA d
letters.value: No accepted value. EVA letters are labels chosen because the glyph looks like them, not sound values.
letters.form: Like a numeral 8 whose top loop is not closed. A small bowl sits at x-height. From its right side a stroke rises above x-height and curls back over to the left, ending in a free tail. The older transcriptions wrote it '8'.
letters.note: Starts the commonest word, 'daiin', and is frequent before y ('dy', 'chedy'). How high the curl rises, and whether it touches the bowl again, should come from the traced folio. The ranking by frequency is approximate and from memory; recount it from a transcription file (Takahashi, or Zandbergen's ZL/IVTFF) before printing any numbers. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: EVA i
letters.value: No accepted value. EVA letters are labels chosen because the glyph looks like them, not sound values.
letters.form: A single short vertical stroke (a minim) at x-height, with no dot and no serif. It comes in runs of one, two or three (rarely four), and each run ends in n, r, l or m.
letters.note: The 'ii' of 'aiin' and 'daiin'. Transcriptions disagree on how many minims some runs have, which is one reason EVA writes them stroke by stroke. The ranking by frequency is approximate and from memory; recount it from a transcription file (Takahashi, or Zandbergen's ZL/IVTFF) before printing any numbers. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: EVA k (gallows)
letters.value: No accepted value. EVA letters are labels chosen because the glyph looks like them, not sound values.
letters.form: A 'gallows' glyph: tall (roughly two to three times x-height), with an upright stem rising from the baseline and a closed loop at the top. Of the four gallows, k and t are the plain forms. I cannot reliably say from memory which side of the stem the loop sits on, or how k differs in detail from t. Do not draw this glyph from this description alone: trace it from the Beinecke's own digital images of MS 408 (the words named in the note are good places to find it), and say which folio the drawing follows.
letters.note: Very common inside words after o or e: 'qokeedy', 'qokedy', 'okaiin', 'chky'. The name 'gallows' is the usual name among researchers; I could not check who coined it. The ranking by frequency is approximate and from memory; recount it from a transcription file (Takahashi, or Zandbergen's ZL/IVTFF) before printing any numbers. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: EVA l
letters.value: No accepted value. EVA letters are labels chosen because the glyph looks like them, not sound values.
letters.form: A glyph with a stroke rising above x-height and a small loop near the baseline, often compared to a cursive Latin l. I am not sure of its exact construction (where the loop closes, and which way the top bends). Do not draw this glyph from this description alone: trace it from the Beinecke's own digital images of MS 408 (the words named in the note are good places to find it), and say which folio the drawing follows.
letters.note: Common at the end of words and before o or k: 'ol', 'al', 'chol', 'shol', 'lkeedy'. On f1r it ends the second word, 'ykal'. The ranking by frequency is approximate and from memory; recount it from a transcription file (Takahashi, or Zandbergen's ZL/IVTFF) before printing any numbers. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: EVA r
letters.value: No accepted value. EVA letters are labels chosen because the glyph looks like them, not sound values.
letters.form: A short glyph at x-height, ending at the baseline, which early transcribers likened to a numeral 2. The form of its top (hook or small loop) is uncertain to me. Do not draw this glyph from this description alone: trace it from the Beinecke's own digital images of MS 408 (the words named in the note are good places to find it), and say which folio the drawing follows.
letters.note: Mostly at the end of words: 'or', 'ar', 'dar', 'chor', 'shory'. letters.name: EVA q
letters.value: No accepted value. EVA letters are labels chosen because the glyph looks like them, not sound values.
letters.form: Like a numeral 4. A diagonal stroke comes down from upper right to lower left, a horizontal stroke runs back to the right, and an upright stem crosses that horizontal. The top of the stem and the top of the diagonal meet in a point or a small closed loop. Its height is about x-height or slightly more; how far the stem descends was not checked.
letters.note: Almost always the first glyph of a word and almost always followed by o: 'qo-' (the '4o' of the older transcriptions), as in 'qokeedy', 'qokain', 'qotedy'. The ranking by frequency is approximate and from memory; recount it from a transcription file (Takahashi, or Zandbergen's ZL/IVTFF) before printing any numbers. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

letters.name: EVA t (gallows)
letters.value: No accepted value. EVA letters are labels chosen because the glyph looks like them, not sound values.
letters.form: The second plain gallows: tall, with an upright stem and a closed loop at the top, like k, but differing from it in the arrangement of its loop or loops. I cannot say from memory exactly how. Do not draw this glyph from this description alone: trace it from the Beinecke's own digital images of MS 408 (the words named in the note are good places to find it), and say which folio the drawing follows.
letters.note: Common inside words: 'qotedy', 'otedy', 'chtey'. It also forms the benched gallows cth (unit 19). The ranking by frequency is approximate and from memory; recount it from a transcription file (Takahashi, or Zandbergen's ZL/IVTFF) before printing any numbers. letters.form: The ch bench (unit 3) with a 'plume': a small curved stroke rising from the top of the left c and arching back over it, above x-height. The rest is as ch.
letters.note: Common at the start of words: 'shedy', 'shol', 'shory'. Whether the plume rises from the left c or from the joining stroke should be checked on the traced folio. letters.name: EVA n
letters.value: No accepted value. EVA letters are labels chosen because the glyph looks like them, not sound values.

letters.note: Almost only at the end of words, after a or i: 'aiin', 'daiin', 'qokaiin', 'ain'. letters.name: EVA s
letters.value: No accepted value. EVA letters are labels chosen because the glyph looks like them, not sound values.
letters.form: Standing alone, it is the left half of sh: a c-curve with the same rising plume. EVA chose the letter so that sh = s + h. I have not seen enough examples to confirm that the alone form is always like that. letters.name: Benched gallows: EVA cth, ckh, cph, cfh
letters.value: No accepted value. EVA letters are labels chosen because the glyph looks like them, not sound values.
letters.form: A gallows glyph drawn over a ch bench. The two c-curves of the bench sit at the foot of the gallows, one on each side of its stem, and the bench's joining stroke runs into or through the stem. EVA spells it c + gallows + h, so that it splits into the same strokes as ch with a gallows inside. Each of the four gallows can be benched. The gallows part has the low confidence of units 8, 12, 16 and 18. Do not draw this glyph from this description alone: trace it from the Beinecke's own digital images of MS 408 (the words named in the note are good places to find it), and say which folio the drawing follows.
letters.note: The arrangement (bench + gallows) is solid; the gallows inside it is not. 'cth' is on f1r line 1; 'ckhy', 'cthy' and 'cphy' are common words. The ranking by frequency is approximate and from memory; recount it from a transcription file (Takahashi, or Zandbergen's ZL/IVTFF) before printing any numbers. lettersSource: THE UNITS ARE EVA GLYPHS, NOT LETTERS WITH VALUES. They are the commonest glyphs of the script, ranked roughly by frequency and labelled in EVA (European/Extensible Voynich Alphabet, Landini and Zandbergen, 1998). EVA spells complex glyphs as strings of simpler strokes (ch, sh, cth). The labels are visual conventions; they claim no sound. The descriptions are from memory of the manuscript and of EVA charts. No plate was checked in this run, because the web-search budget had run out. Forms marked 'low' (the four gallows, l, r, n, s, m and the rare glyphs) must be traced from the Beinecke's digital images of MS 408, citing the folio. Good places to look: f1r line 1 (f, y, k, l, a, r, i, n, sh, o, cth) and the 'qokeedy'/'daiin' pages of the bathing (biological) section (q, o, k, e, d, y, a, i, n). Do not draw from modern Voynich fonts without checking them against the manuscript.

uses.use: Writing the whole text of MS 408: herbal, astronomical and astrological, 'balneological' (bathing), cosmological, pharmaceutical and 'recipe' sections
uses.evidence: The conventional section names come from the pictures, not from any reading of the text (D'Imperio 1978; Zandbergen). Approximate ranges: herbal ff. 1–66; astronomical and zodiac ff. 67–73; bathing ff. 75–84; the 'rosettes' foldout ff. 85–86; pharmaceutical ff. 87–102; short starred paragraphs ff. 103–116. These ranges are from memory; check them against the Beinecke foliation. Whether the book was ever used as a working herbal or medical handbook is unknown. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

Single Voynich words stand beside plants, jars, stars and figures, especially in the pharmaceutical and astronomical sections. Because a label ought to name its picture, readers such as Bax (2014) have built their proposed readings on them. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

uses.use: A prized curiosity in early-modern Prague and Rome
uses.evidence: Baresch's letter of 1639 and Marci's of 1665/6 show learned owners trying to get the book read, and treating Kircher, known for his work on Coptic and hieroglyphs, as the man to do it. The story of 600 ducats (attributed) shows how highly it was valued. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

uses.use: A test case for 20th-century cryptanalysis and later for computational linguistics
uses.evidence: The Friedman study groups (1944–46, 1962–63), the NSA work of Tiltman, Currier and D'Imperio (1967–78), and statistical and machine-learning studies since 1998, all of which use EVA-based transcription files. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

Researchers write, search and count the text in EVA, quoting words such as 'daiin' or 'qokeedy'. EVA was designed so that transcribers would not have to settle in advance which strokes make one glyph (Landini and Zandbergen 1998). It is a tool for transcription, not a reading. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

quotations.text: Dr. Raphael Ferdinandi tertii tum Regis Boemiae in lingua Boemica instructor dicti libri fuisse Rudolphi Imperatoris, pro quo ipse latori qui librum attulisset 600 ducatos persolverit. Authorem autem esse putabat Rogerium Bacconem Anglum.
quotations.translation: Latin original, as it is usually transcribed, given from memory. Collate it with the letter, or a published transcription, before printing. My own paraphrase, not a published translation: 'Dr Raphael, who taught the Bohemian language to Ferdinand III, then King of Bohemia, [said] that the book had belonged to the Emperor Rudolf, who paid the man who brought it 600 ducats; and he thought the author was the Englishman Roger Bacon.'
quotations.source: Johannes Marcus Marci to Athanasius Kircher, Prague, 19 August 1665 or 1666; the letter is kept with Beinecke MS 408. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

quotations.text: The Voynich MSS was an early attempt to construct an artificial or universal language of the a priori type.
quotations.source: William F. Friedman. He hid this sentence in an anagram, printed in 1959, as I recall in W. F. and E. S. Friedman, 'Acrostics, Anagrams, and Chaucer', Philological Quarterly 38. The solution was made public after his death in 1969. It is quoted, among other places, in D'Imperio 1978. The publication details are at medium-low confidence; verify them before printing. Basis: my prior knowledge; not re-checked in this run (the shared web-search budget was used up before this item began).

links.relation: The Latin-script additions in the manuscript (month names, the last-page lines on f. 116v), Marci's Latin letter, and the 'abbreviated Latin' hypotheses (Feely 1943, Gibbs 2017).
One of the natural-language proposals (Hauer and Kondrak 2016–2018). The Hebrew hall can show why a computer 'match' to Hebrew is not a reading.
Kircher's Coptic work (Prodromus coptus, 1636) is why Baresch and Marci sent the manuscript to him in Rome.

Context: Trithemius's Steganographia (written c. 1499) and Polygraphia (1518) show what learned secret writing looked like about a century after the vellum was made. No connection with the Voynich script is documented.

The Dee and Kelley hypothesis (disputed): Voynich's conjecture that Dee sold the book to Rudolf II, and suggestions that Kelley forged it. The Enochian alphabet is another invented script from the same circle, but has a documented origin (1583).
Contrast: a secret alphabet with a known key and a known printed source, beside a script with neither.

The zodiac pages (ff. 70v–73v, approximately) have a picture of each sign (ram, bull and so on) at the centre of the medallion. As I recall, they do not use the astrological sign-glyphs; check this on the pages before the comparison is drawn.

cautions: Never print a 'translation' or 'reading' of any Voynich word as if it were established. Every proposed reading is disputed. EVA words such as 'daiin' are transcription labels, not pronunciations.
Radiocarbon dates the vellum, not the writing. Write 'the vellum has been dated to 1404–1438', not 'the manuscript was written in 1404–1438'.
Rudolf II, the 600 ducats and Roger Bacon all come from one hearsay report in Marci's letter. Write 'Marci reports that Raphael Mnishovsky told him…', never 'Rudolf II bought it'.

Dee's ownership is a conjecture; there is no document behind it. Kelley's or Voynich's authorship is a hoax hypothesis; there is no document behind it either. Report them as such, with the objections.

The manuscript is not documented as having been used for magic. It belongs in the Magical Scriptorium because it is a secret or unknown script with astrological and herbal pictures, and the page should say so plainly.

LETTER FORMS: the four gallows (k, t, p, f), l, r, n, s, m and the rare glyphs are graded 'low'. Trace them from the Beinecke's images of MS 408, citing the folio, or leave a gap. A wrong glyph shown as 'Voynichese' is worse than none.
Transcriptions disagree on word spaces, on how many i-minims a run has, and on rare glyphs. When the page quotes an EVA word, name the transcription (Takahashi, or Zandbergen's ZL).

Folio ranges for the sections, the list of missing leaves, Baresch's death date and the 1639 letter's day are from memory. Check them against the Beinecke catalogue, Clemens (ed.) 2016 or voynich.nu before printing.

Images: use the Beinecke's own digital images, and check Yale's terms of use. I recall an open-access policy for public-domain works, but did not check it this run. Do not use the 2016 Yale facsimile's or other facsimiles' reproductions without permission.
Keep sensational claims (aliens, lost civilisations) off the page. They are not scholarship, and the house rule is to report traditions without mocking them; such claims are not a tradition.

confidence: SOLID (standard facts, though not re-checked in this run): the shelfmark Beinecke MS 408; Kraus's gift to Yale in 1969; the radiocarbon date of 1404–1438 (University of Arizona, samples 2009, announced 2011); Marci's letter to Kircher, dated 19 August 1665 or 1666, and its report of Rudolf II, 600 ducats and Roger Bacon; Voynich's purchase from the Jesuits at the Villa Mondragone in 1912; Newbold's claim and Manly's refutation; the Friedman study groups; Currier A and B; D'Imperio 1978; EVA by Landini and Zandbergen (1998); the four hypotheses and the main published proposals for each; the absence of any accepted decipherment. FAIRLY SURE: Baresch's letter of 1639 (the day, 27 April, less so); the Horcicky inscription and the 1608 ennoblement; the Collegio Romano and Beckx stage; the section names; the forms of o, a, y, i, q, d, e, ch and sh, and the bench-plus-gallows layout. SHAKY: the list of missing folios and the section folio ranges; Baresch's death about 1662; the price Kraus paid; the Dee diary entry of 630 ducats; the details of where Friedman's anagram was published; the exact Latin of Marci's sentence; journal volume and issue numbers. LETTER FORMS: ten of the twenty units are 'low', namely the four gallows, l, r, n, s, m and the rare-glyph card; trace them from the Beinecke images. No search results were available for this item (the shared web-search budget was used up before it began), so everything here is from my prior knowledge. Only one URL is given (the voynich.nu home page, a well-known domain); no other URL could be checked.
